questions.q: The transfer of heat from the hotter part of an object to its colder part is called
questions.a: Conduction (p. 91). Convection is heat carried by moving particles of liquids and gases; radiation needs no medium; infiltration is water seeping into the ground.
o: conduction
convection
radiation
infiltration

o: They pass heat to their neighbours but stay in their own positions
They move from the hot end to the cold end carrying the heat
They leave the solid at the hot end and re-enter at the cold end
They stay still and let heat jump across the gaps between them

questions.q: In Activity 7.1, pin I (nearest the candle flame) falls before pin II. Which statement gives the reason?

o: Heat reaches the wax of pin I first and melts it before the heat has travelled on to pin II

Hot particles of the strip travel to pin I and push that pin off the strip before the others
Hot air rising from the flame pushes pin I off the strip well before it reaches the other pins

questions.q: Which statement about conduction is FALSE?

Heat flows from the hotter part of the object to its colder part

Conduction needs matter whose particles pass on the heat

questions.q: Meera stirs boiling kheer with a steel spoon. After a few minutes the end she is holding becomes warm. Which statement explains this?
questions.a: This is conduction along a solid. The travelling-particles option is wrong because particles stay in position; the rising-air option is convection of air; the empty-space option is a radiation-style explanation that ignores the spoon.
o: Each heated particle of the spoon passes heat to its neighbour all along the handle
Hot steel particles slowly travel up the handle from the kheer to reach her hand
Hot air rising from the kheer carries the heat straight up the handle to her hand
Heat crosses the empty space between the kheer and her hand without any medium

questions.q: Palden repeats Activity 7.1 with a strip of wood of the same size in place of the metal strip, using the same wax, pins and candle. What will he most likely see?

questions.q:
Read the statements.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Activity 7.1 the pins fall one after another, starting with the pin nearest the flame.
Reason (R): In conduction the particles of the strip travel along it from the hot end and carry the heat with them.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the particles pass heat to neighbours but do not move from their positions.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: (a) Define conduction. (b) Using your definition, explain why the end of an iron tongs, left in a coal fire, becomes too hot to hold.
questions.a: (a) Conduction is the transfer of heat from the hotter part of an object to its colder part, each heated particle passing heat to its neighbour while staying in its position. (b) Heat passes from particle to particle along the iron tongs from the end in the fire to the handle end.
s: Part (a): heat passes from hotter to colder part, particle to neighbour, without particles moving
Part (b): heat passed along the iron from the fire end to the hand end

questions.q: Two rods of equal size, one of iron and one of dry wood, each have one end held in a candle flame for a minute. (a) Which rod's far end will feel warmer when touched? (b) Give the reason in terms of conductors.
questions.a: (a) The iron rod. (b) Iron is a good conductor and lets heat pass easily along it; wood is a poor conductor and does not.
s: Part (a): the iron rod's far end is warmer
Part (b): iron is a good conductor, wood a poor conductor

questions.q: A student holds the far end of an iron rod while the other end rests in a flame. After a while the end in her hand grows hot, though no part of the rod has moved. (a) Name the process. (b) Explain how the heat reached her hand.
questions.a: (a) Conduction. (b) Each heated particle passed the heat to the next particle in contact, and so on along the rod, without the particles leaving their positions.
s: Part (a): names conduction
Part (b): heat passed from particle to neighbouring particle with no particle moving away

questions.q: State two things that conduction needs, using the ideas of the chapter.
questions.a: A hotter part and a colder part of the object, so that heat can pass from the hotter to the colder part; and a medium, that is, matter whose particles pass the heat on.
s: Names the hotter-to-colder direction of heat transfer
Names the need for a medium of particles

questions.q: (a) Name the process by which heat passes from the flame through an iron tava to the roti lying on it. (b) The tava does not move, yet the roti side gets hot; what happens to the particles of the tava?
questions.a: (a) Conduction. (b) Each heated particle passes heat to its neighbour up to the roti side, while the particles stay in their positions.
s: Part (a): conduction
Part (b): particles pass heat to neighbours and do not move away

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'When one end of a metal rod is heated, heat travels along the rod to the far end by conduction. This happens because the hot particles move along the rod to the cold end.' Is Ishaan right? Say whether he is right, partly right or wrong, and explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Heat does travel along the rod to the far end by conduction, but the reason given is wrong: in conduction the particles do not move from their positions. The heated particle passes heat to its neighbour, and so on, so the heat travels though the particles stay put.
s: Verdict: partly right (heat does travel by conduction, but the reason is wrong)
Particles stay in their positions during conduction
Far end warms because heat is passed neighbour to neighbour

questions.q: Describe one everyday situation, not given in the chapter, in which heat travels by conduction. Say which part is hotter, which part gains heat, and what the particles do.
questions.a: Example: a steel tumbler of hot tea warms the hand held round it. The tea and tumbler wall are hotter, the hand gains heat, and the particles of the steel pass heat to neighbours without leaving their positions. Any valid example with the three points earns full marks.
s: A valid everyday situation of conduction
Hotter part and the part gaining heat identified
Particles pass heat on without moving from their positions

questions.q: Pema changes the set-up of Activity 7.1: she keeps the strip and four pins but heats the end that is near the stand, which is the end close to pin IV (pin I is at the other end). (a) Which pin falls first? (b) Which falls last? (c) Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Pin IV. (b) Pin I. (c) Heat travels along the strip from the heated end, so it reaches the wax of the nearest pin first and the farthest pin last.
s: Part (a): pin IV falls first
Part (b): pin I falls last
Part (c): heat travels from the heated end, nearest pin first

questions.q: A cook holds a long iron tongs in a coal fire. (i) Explain how heat reaches her hand, saying what the particles do. (ii) Explain what changes if the tongs have a wooden grip. (iii) Say which tongs she should prefer and give a reason.
questions.a: (i) Heat passes from particle to neighbouring particle along the iron, from the hot end to the colder end; the particles stay in their positions. (ii) Wood is a poor conductor, so the grip does not let heat pass easily to her hand. (iii) She should prefer the tongs with the wooden grip because the grip stays cool enough to hold.
s: Names conduction as the way heat travels along the iron
Particles pass heat on but do not move from their positions
Wood is a poor conductor and passes heat slowly
States that the hand is protected at the grip
Prefers the tongs with a wooden grip with reason

questions.q: A student claims that the Sun's heat reaches the Earth by conduction. Evaluate this claim using what conduction needs, say which process the book gives for the Sun's heat, and give one example where conduction does take place.
questions.a: Conduction needs a medium, matter whose particles pass the heat on, and works from particle to neighbouring particle. The book says the Sun's heat reaches the Earth by radiation, which needs no medium. So the claim is not correct. An example of conduction: heat travelling along a metal strip or a spoon in hot tea.
s: States that conduction needs a medium of particles
Notes that radiation needs no medium
Names radiation as the process for the Sun's heat
Gives a correct example of conduction
Final verdict: the claim is wrong

questions.q:
The canteen of a school in Nagpur tests three spoons of equal length for stirring a pot of boiling sambar. After two minutes in the pot, the handle end of each spoon is measured. Spoon P (all steel, Rs 40 each): 61 degrees Celsius. Spoon Q (steel with a wooden handle, Rs 65 each): 34. Spoon R (all wood, Rs 90 each): 33. The room is at 30 degrees Celsius.
(a) How many degrees above the room temperature is the handle end of each spoon?
(b) Explain the reading of spoon P, naming the process.
(c) Explain why the handle ends of Q and R stayed cool.

questions.a: (a) P 31, Q 4, R 3 degrees Celsius. (b) Conduction: steel is a good conductor, so heat passed from particle to particle up the handle. (c) Wood is a poor conductor, so little heat reached the handle end. (d) 12 of P cost Rs 480, Q Rs 780, R Rs 1,080. R is over budget. P fits but its handle gets too hot; Q fits the budget and has a cool handle, so recommend Q.
s: Part (a): 31, 4 and 3 degrees Celsius
Part (b): conduction in a good conductor
Part (c): wood is a poor conductor
Part (d): costs 480, 780, 1,080 and recommends Q within budget with its cool handle

questions.q:
Two friends test rods of equal size by putting wax dots at 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm from the end that is heated by a flame. On rod X the dots melt at 45 s, 100 s and 170 s. On rod Y the 5 cm dot melts at 3 minutes, while the other two dots are still unmelted after 10 minutes.
(a) Which rod is the better conductor, and how many seconds after the first dot did the second dot melt on rod X?
(b) Explain, in terms of particles, how the heat reached the 15 cm dot on rod X.
(c) What does the melting of Y's 5 cm dot show about heat in a poor conductor?
(d) A cook needs one of these rods for the base of a pan and one for its handle. Which rod should be used for each part, and why?
questions.a: (a) Rod X; 100 - 45 = 55 seconds. (b) Each heated particle passed the heat to its neighbour along the rod without moving from its position. (c) A poor conductor lets heat through only with difficulty, so it travels slowly and reaches only a short distance. (d) Rod X for the base, because a good conductor passes heat to the food; rod Y for the handle, because a poor conductor does not let heat reach the hand quickly.
s: Part (a): rod X, and 55 seconds
Part (b): heat passed neighbour to neighbour with particles staying in position
Part (c): a poor conductor passes heat only slowly and with difficulty
Part (d): X for the base, Y for the handle, each with a conductor reason

questions.q: Which of the following materials is a good conductor of heat?
questions.a: Metals such as iron are good conductors (p. 91). Glass, wood and clay are the book's examples of poor conductors.

Wood

questions.a: The book gives this reason on p. 91. questions.a: Clay and porcelain are poor conductors of heat (p. 91). are good conductors, so they spread the heat evenly through the drink
trap air in their pores in the same way as woollen cloth does

o: Wool is a good conductor and carries our body heat away evenly
Woollen fabric traps air in its tiny pores and keeps it there
Air trapped in the wool is a poor conductor of heat in general
Heat flow from our body to the surroundings is reduced greatly

questions.q: Sunita wraps a steel tiffin box of hot rotis in a woollen shawl for a train journey, and the rotis stay warm for much longer. Which idea explains this?
questions.a: The book says woollen fabric traps air in its pores and air is a poor conductor, which reduces heat flow (p. 92). The other statements give wool a property the book does not give it.
o: Air trapped in the wool is a poor conductor, so less heat flows out of the box
Wool is a good conductor and spreads the heat of the rotis evenly in the box
Wool reflects most of the heat of the rotis back into the steel tiffin box
Wool produces heat of its own that adds to the warmth of the hot rotis

questions.q: Aarav's mother says two thin blankets will keep him warmer than one thick blanket. Which statement gives the correct reason?
questions.a: The book says the air between two thin blankets is the reason for preferring them (p. 92). The other options treat the blankets or the gap as good conductors.
o: Air trapped between the two thin blankets is a poor conductor and cuts down heat loss
Thin cloth is a good conductor, so it passes the warmth of the room on to his body
Heat moves faster between two blankets, so his body is warmed up much sooner
Two blankets together form a better conductor of heat than one thick blanket does

Read the statements.

questions.a: All three statements are correct (pp. 91-92): air is a poor conductor, trapped air in hollow bricks slows heat flow in both seasons, and clay and porcelain are poor conductors.

1 and 2 only

questions.q:

questions.q:
Match the use in Column I with the reason in Column II.

questions.q: (a) Name two good conductors and two poor conductors of heat from the chapter. (b) Which type would you use for the handle of a frying pan?
questions.a: (a) Good: iron, aluminium (metals). Poor: wood, glass, clay, porcelain (any two). (b) A poor conductor such as wood, so the heat of the pan does not pass quickly to the hand.

Part (b): a poor conductor, with a reason

questions.q: (a) Why does woollen fabric help to keep us warm? (b) Use your answer to explain why air trapped between layers of clothing also keeps us warm.

s: Part (a): wool traps air, and air is a poor conductor
Part (b): air between layers acts as a poor conductor, reducing heat loss

Poor conductor (insulator) defined with a use

States that air is a poor conductor

Wool traps air in its pores

Clay or porcelain (poor conductors) keep tea hot longer
Concludes that the shopkeeper's reasoning is wrong

questions.a: (i) Metal is a good conductor so the pan heats food; wood is a poor conductor so the handle does not pass heat to the hand. (ii) Clay is a poor conductor, so tea stays hot longer. (iii) Wool traps air, a poor conductor, which reduces heat flow from the body.

(ii) clay cup: poor conductor keeps tea hot
(iii) wool traps air, reducing heat loss

questions.a: (i) Metal utensils conduct heat to the food; clay and porcelain cups, being poor conductors, keep tea or coffee hot longer. (ii) Woollen fabric traps air in its pores; air is a poor conductor, so heat flow from the body is reduced; two thin blankets with air between them are warmer than one thick blanket. s: Utensils and cups: good and poor conductors used with reason
Clothing: wool traps air

questions.a: A: wood and mud are poor conductors, so they prevent heat loss and keep the room warm; cost 60 x 1,100 = Rs 66,000, within budget. Recommend A, since it suits winter use and fits the firm budget; B's summer benefit does not matter for a winter-use room.
s: Wood and mud in A are poor conductors that prevent heat loss
Trapped air in B's hollow bricks is a poor conductor
Costs worked out: Rs 66,000 and Rs 84,000
Compares fit to budget and to winter use
Recommends A with the reasons

questions.q:
At a 12-day winter fair in Mussoorie, Meena serves 200 cups of tea a day. She pours tea at 80 degrees Celsius. Ten minutes later the tea measures 52 degrees in a steel tumbler and 66 degrees in a clay kulhad. A steel tumbler costs Rs 22 and can be reused all 12 days, while a kulhad costs Rs 3 and is thrown away after one use.
(a) By how many degrees did the tea cool in each cup?
(b) Explain the difference using the idea of conductors.
(c) Meena suggests tying a woollen cover round each steel tumbler. Would that help? Explain.
(d) Work out the cost of tumblers (200, bought once) and of kulhads for the 12 days, and decide which she should use.
questions.a: (a) Tumbler 80 - 52 = 28; kulhad 80 - 66 = 14 degrees Celsius. (b) Steel is a good conductor and lets heat out quickly; clay is a poor conductor and lets it out slowly. (c) Yes: wool traps air in its pores, air is a poor conductor, so less heat flows out of the tumbler. (d) Tumblers 200 x 22 = Rs 4,400; kulhads 200 x 3 x 12 = Rs 7,200. Tumblers cost Rs 2,800 less but cool the tea 14 degrees more; a covered tumbler (c) keeps the saving and reduces the cooling, so choose tumblers with woollen covers (a kulhad choice is acceptable if justified by the hotter tea).
s: Part (a): 28 and 14 degrees Celsius
Part (b): steel good conductor, clay poor conductor
Part (c): wool traps air, a poor conductor, so less heat flows out
Part (d): Rs 4,400 and Rs 7,200 and a decision weighing cost against hot tea

questions.q:

House X, with walls of two wooden layers filled with cow dung and mud, is at 14 degrees and cost Rs 2,40,000. House Y, built with hollow bricks, is at 13 degrees and cost Rs 1,90,000. questions.a: (a) 14 - 5 = 9 degrees Celsius. (b) House Z; iron is a good conductor, so heat passes out quickly. (c) The air trapped in the hollow bricks is a poor conductor, so little heat escapes. (d) House Y: it is only 1 degree cooler than X inside and costs Rs 50,000 less, within the Rs 2,00,000 budget; X is over budget.
s: Part (a): 9 degrees Celsius
Part (b): Z, with iron a good conductor
Part (c): trapped air is a poor conductor
Part (d): Y, weighing 1 degree against Rs 50,000 and the budget

questions.q:
A family in Kullu keeps a bukhari in its winter room. It is an iron stove burning wood, with a long iron pipe on top that vents out the smoke and a flat top for a kettle. The hot air from the stove rises straight to the ceiling and does not blow towards the family. The children sit two metres to the side and feel warm on their faces. A thermometer reads 70 degrees Celsius on the pipe just above the stove and 38 degrees Celsius two metres up the pipe.
(a) Name the process by which heat passes from the hot iron top to the base of the kettle.
(b) Name the process by which the children feel the warmth on their faces, and say why it cannot be conduction or convection.
(c) Which process carries heat along the iron pipe, and what do the readings show about its direction?
(d) Palden says: 'The bukhari warms the room by radiation alone.' Judge this using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Conduction. (b) Radiation: the warmth comes directly from the hot stove; air is a poor conductor and no hot air blows to the children, so conduction and convection do not explain it. (c) Conduction along the iron pipe; heat flows from the hotter part near the stove towards the cooler part higher up. (d) Not correct: the bukhari involves all three processes: conduction to the kettle and pipe, radiation to the children, and convection by the moving hot air and smoke.
s: Part (a): conduction
Part (b): radiation, with reasons excluding conduction and convection
Part (c): conduction, heat flowing from hotter to cooler part
Part (d): rejects 'radiation alone' since all three processes act

questions.q:
The sports committee of a Jaipur school tests two identical cotton T-shirts, one white and one black, on a May afternoon. Both are kept in the shade of the tent at 38 degrees Celsius, then spread in the Sun for 30 minutes. The white one then reads 42 and the black one reads 52. The school's house team, Shivaji House, wants black T-shirts for its identity. The committee can choose black T-shirts, or white T-shirts with a black band.
(a) Find the rise in temperature for each.
(b) How many degrees hotter is the black T-shirt than the white one?
(c) Explain the difference with the ideas of reflection and absorption of heat.
(d) Which option should the committee choose for the May sports day? Weigh team identity against comfort.
questions.a: (a) White 42 - 38 = 4; black 52 - 38 = 14 degrees Celsius. (b) 52 - 42 = 10 degrees Celsius. (c) The white one reflects most of the heat falling on it, while the black one absorbs more. (d) White with a black band: light-coloured clothes are more comfortable in summer, and the band keeps the team's black identity, so comfort is not sacrificed.
s: Part (a): 4 and 14 degrees Celsius
Part (b): 10 degrees Celsius
Part (c): light reflects, dark absorbs
Part (d): white with band, weighing identity against comfort using (c)

questions.q: What is precipitation?
questions.a: Clouds bring rain, snow and hail; this is precipitation (p. 98). The option 'Water leaving trees and plants as vapour' is transpiration, the option 'Water seeping through soil and rocks into the ground' infiltration, the option 'Water vapour cooling to form clouds' condensation.
o: Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail
Water leaving trees and plants as vapour
Water seeping through soil and rocks into the ground
Water vapour cooling to form clouds

questions.q: In Activity 7.5, in which order does water seep through the materials, from fastest to slowest?
questions.a: Water seeps fastest through gravel, slower through sand and slowest through clay (p. 100). The other options swap the materials.
o: Gravel, sand, clay
Clay, sand, gravel
Sand, gravel, clay
Gravel, clay, sand

questions.q: Water seeps fastest through gravel because
questions.a: The spaces between gravel particles are wider (p. 100). The tinier-particles and wider-clay-spaces options reverse the sizes; the soaking-up option gives a reason that is not in the book.
o: the spaces between gravel particles are wider than the spaces in sand and clay
the particles of gravel are much tinier than the particles of sand and clay
gravel particles soak up the water and pass it on to the layer below them
the spaces in clay are wider than those in gravel, so water gets stuck there

questions.q: Which statement about groundwater is NOT correct?
questions.a: The book says groundwater is not unlimited and is getting depleted by excessive extraction (p. 100). The statement that it is unlimited is the incorrect one.
o: Groundwater is unlimited, so it can be drawn out without any care
It is stored in the pore spaces of sediments and openings in rocks
Recharge pits help to replenish it
It is the water we draw out through wells and bore wells

questions.q: In a rapidly growing town in Maharashtra, roads and courtyards are covered with concrete and trees have been cut. Wells are drying up even in good rainy seasons. Which statement best explains this?
questions.a: The book names decreased vegetation cover and increased concrete surfaces as limiting infiltration (p. 100). The other options are false or reverse how water moves through clay.
o: Concrete and fewer plants limit infiltration, so less rainwater reaches the aquifers
Heavy rain has stopped the water cycle, so no rainwater is reaching the ground now
Concrete has made the spaces between soil particles wider, so water drains away fast
Clay has replaced the gravel under the town, so water seeps faster and is then lost

questions.q: Rahul repeats Activity 7.5 with three unlabelled bottles, each holding clay, sand or gravel, and 200 mL of water in each. After 10 minutes the beakers hold 15 mL (bottle P), 150 mL (bottle Q) and 70 mL (bottle R). Which bottle most likely holds sand?
questions.a: Gravel gives the most (Q), clay the least (P), and sand lies between (R) (p. 100). The options 'Bottle P, as sand is the material that lets least water t...' and 'Bottle Q, as sand lets the most water seep through' name the clay and gravel bottles; the option 'Any of them, as all three get 200 mL of water' ignores the data.
o: Bottle R, as sand seeps faster than clay but slower than gravel
Bottle P, as sand is the material that lets least water through
Bottle Q, as sand lets the most water seep through
Any of them, as all three get 200 mL of water

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Infiltration is the seeping of surface water through soil and rocks.
Statement 2: Water seeps fastest through clay and slowest through gravel.
Statement 3: Groundwater, once used, is never replenished by the water cycle.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is false: water seeps fastest through gravel and slowest through clay. Statement 3 is false: the water cycle recharges groundwater sources, which rainwater harvesting and recharge pits also replenish.
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Groundwater is getting depleted in many places.
Reason (R): The water cycle conserves the total amount of water on the Earth.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. But the water cycle conserving the total water does not explain depletion; the book blames excessive extraction and less infiltration.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

questions.q: (a) Name two ways in which water vapour gets into the air. (b) What happens to the vapour when it rises?
questions.a: (a) Evaporation from oceans, rivers and lakes, and transpiration from trees and plants. (b) It cools down and condenses to form clouds.
s: Part (a): evaporation and transpiration
Part (b): cools and condenses into clouds

questions.q: (a) Define infiltration. (b) Which would let rainwater reach groundwater faster, gravel or clay, and why?
questions.a: (a) Infiltration is the seeping of surface water through soil and rocks. (b) Gravel, because the spaces between its particles are wider than in clay.
s: Part (a): surface water seeping through soil and rocks
Part (b): gravel, as its spaces are wider

questions.q: What are aquifers, and how do people use the water stored in them?
questions.a: Aquifers are underground layers of sediments and rocks that store water in pore spaces. People draw this water by digging wells or drilling bore wells into them.
s: Aquifers store water in pore spaces of underground layers
Water is extracted by wells and bore wells

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why groundwater is getting depleted.
questions.a: Growing water requirements of an increasing population lead to excessive extraction; decreased vegetation cover and more concrete surfaces limit water infiltration.
s: Excessive extraction due to a growing population
Less vegetation and more concrete limiting infiltration

questions.q: (a) Why do wet clothes dry faster on a sunny day? (b) Name the stage of the water cycle that the drying of clothes resembles when it happens in oceans and lakes.
questions.a: (a) The heat from the Sun makes the evaporation of water faster. (b) Evaporation.
s: Part (a): the Sun's heat makes evaporation faster
Part (b): evaporation

questions.q: Neha says: 'Some rain that falls on the ground flows into rivers and the sea, and some seeps into the ground. The water that seeps in is stored underground and can never be used by us.' Is Neha right? Say whether she is right, partly right or wrong, and explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Some rainwater flows into ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans and some seeps into the ground by infiltration, but the stored groundwater can be used: it collects in aquifers, from which wells and handpumps draw water.
s: Verdict: partly right (seepage is correct, but the water is usable)
Some rainwater seeps into the ground by infiltration
It is stored as groundwater in aquifers, from which wells and handpumps draw water

questions.q: Show why continuous evaporation of water from oceans, rivers and lakes does not use up the Earth's water.
questions.a: The water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds. Precipitation brings it back down as rain, snow and hail, and it flows through soil, rocks and plants to return to water bodies. The water cycle conserves the total amount of water on the Earth.
s: Vapour condenses into clouds
Precipitation returns the water to the Earth
Water returns to water bodies; the cycle conserves the total water

questions.q: In Activity 7.5, 200 mL of water is poured into each bottle. In 10 minutes the beakers collect 20 mL (clay), 90 mL (sand) and 160 mL (gravel). (a) How much water is still in each bottle? (b) Which material would help most in recharging groundwater? (c) Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Clay 180 mL, sand 110 mL, gravel 40 mL. (b) Gravel. (c) The spaces between its particles are wider, so water seeps through more easily.
s: Part (a): 180, 110 and 40 mL
Part (b): gravel
Part (c): wider spaces between particles

questions.q: Describe the water cycle, and say how it helps the Earth.
questions.a: The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers and lakes, and it evaporates; plants also release water by transpiration. Water vapour rises, cools and condenses to form clouds. Clouds bring rain, snow and hail by precipitation. The water passes through soil, rocks and plants and returns to water bodies. The water cycle redistributes and replenishes water and conserves the total amount of water on the Earth.
s: Evaporation by the Sun's heat and transpiration
Condensation of vapour into clouds
Precipitation as rain, snow and hail
Water returns through soil, rocks and plants to water bodies
Redistributes, replenishes and conserves water

questions.q: One village has mostly sandy soil and another mostly clay soil. The same rain falls on both. Predict which village will recharge its groundwater faster, explain why, say what may happen to the rest of the rainwater in the other village, and suggest one measure to recharge groundwater there.
questions.a: The sandy village recharges faster: water seeps more readily through sand than through clay because the spaces between sand particles are wider. In the clay village water seeps slowest, so rainwater can flow into ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans instead of seeping. The clay village can use rainwater harvesting or recharge pits to replenish groundwater.
s: Predicts the sandy village recharges faster
Reason: wider spaces between sand particles than clay
Clay seeps slowest, so water seeps in less
Rest of the rain flows to ponds, lakes and rivers
A recharge measure such as pits or rainwater harvesting

questions.q:
A village in Satara depends on one open well. Records show that the water level stood 8 metres below the ground in 2015 and 21 metres below the ground in 2025, though the yearly rainfall was about the same. Over these years the village square and lanes were covered with concrete. The panchayat has Rs 1,50,000. It can build recharge pits near the square for Rs 1,20,000, or lay a pipeline to bring water from a river 12 km away for Rs 9,00,000.
(a) By how many metres has the water level fallen?
(b) Explain why paving the square could lower the well level though the rainfall stayed the same.
(c) Explain how recharge pits help the aquifer.
(d) Which option should the panchayat choose? Weigh the budget and the long-term effect on groundwater.
questions.a: (a) 21 - 8 = 13 metres. (b) Concrete limits infiltration, so less rainwater seeps down to refill the aquifer. (c) Recharge pits let rainwater infiltrate into the ground and replenish the aquifer. (d) The recharge pits: Rs 1,20,000 is within the Rs 1,50,000 budget, while the pipeline costs Rs 9,00,000 and does not refill the village's own groundwater. The pits give water back only slowly after rain, so the panchayat should also limit extraction meanwhile.
s: Part (a): 13 metres
Part (b): concrete limits infiltration
Part (c): rainwater infiltrates and replenishes the aquifer
Part (d): recharge pits, weighing budget and groundwater recovery

questions.q:
In a Ladakh village the streams dry up in spring. During winter the villagers channel stream water down underground pipes and spray it into the cold air, where it freezes layer by layer into a tall cone, an ice stupa. The stupa holds 1,50,000 litres of water as ice. The fields need 2,500 litres a day in spring and the dry spell lasts 90 days.
(a) For how many days will the stupa's water last?
(b) Why do the streams dry up in spring, and when does the stupa melt?
(c) How many more litres are needed to cover the 90 days?
(d) The village can build a second stupa for the shortfall, or cut daily use so that 1,50,000 litres lasts 90 days. Find that daily amount to the nearest 10 litres and recommend one option.
questions.a: (a) 1,50,000 / 2,500 = 60 days. (b) The heat from the Sun's radiation is not enough to melt the snow on the mountains; the stupa melts slowly during spring, providing water. (c) 90 x 2,500 = 2,25,000 litres needed; 2,25,000 - 1,50,000 = 75,000 litres more. (d) 1,50,000 / 90 = about 1,670 litres a day, which is about 830 litres (one third) less than 2,500. A second stupa of 75,000 litres keeps full supply to the fields; cutting use by a third saves effort but may harm crops. Either recommendation is acceptable if it uses these numbers.
s: Part (a): 60 days
Part (b): the Sun's heat does not melt the mountain snow in spring; the stupa melts slowly in spring
Part (c): 75,000 litres more
Part (d): about 1,670 litres a day and a recommendation weighing both options
